## Causal inference and the counterfactual

**Difference-in-differences** (hereafter **DiD**) is a method of **causal inference** — it
identifies a cause-and-effect relationship. It turns on one question:
*what would have happened had the shock or policy never occurred?* From that
**counterfactual** we recover the effect of the shock or the policy.

Science fiction is built on the same question — stories of an alternative history or a
parallel world: *The Man in the High Castle* (P. K. Dick), *Back to the Future*,
*Doctor Strange* (Marvel), and many more.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig/sc_fi.png}
\end{center}

## What is difference-in-differences?

An exogenous shock (a reform, a natural disaster, a price change) hits one group of units,
the **treated group**, at a known date. A second group with similar characteristics, the
**control group**, is not hit. Both groups are observed **before** and **after** the date,
in a panel or in repeated cross-sections.

\begin{block}{The method}
The effect of the shock is the \textbf{change} in the outcome of the treated group minus
the \textbf{change} in the outcome of the control group.
\end{block}

- In a regression, simple DiD is the TWFE model of the panel chapter with one additional
  regressor, a dummy equal to 1 for treated units after the shock.

## The origin: John Snow and cholera (1855)

\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig/map_snow.png}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
\small
\textbf{Origin: epidemiology} --- the fight against cholera in London. Cholera was assumed
to be transmitted by \textbf{air}; John Snow (1855) argued instead that it came from
\textbf{infected water}.

\medskip
\textbf{How to prove it?} A \emph{natural experiment}. The whole city drew water from the
same point in the Thames, until a reform split the supply: some districts now received
water from \textbf{downstream} of the sewers (infected), others from \textbf{upstream}
(assumed uncontaminated).

\medskip
$\Rightarrow$ \emph{treated vs control}, \emph{before vs after} --- the first
difference-in-differences.
\end{column}
\end{columns}

# The $2\times2$

## Potential outcomes and the missing counterfactual

Each unit $i$ has two potential outcomes: $Y_i(1)$ **if treated**, $Y_i(0)$ **if not**.
The treatment indicator $D_i\in\{0,1\}$ selects the one we observe, and the causal effect
is the gap between the two:
$$ Y_i = D_i\,Y_i(1)+(1-D_i)\,Y_i(0), \qquad \tau_i = Y_i(1)-Y_i(0). $$

\begin{alertblock}{The fundamental problem of causal inference}
For any unit we observe \textbf{only one} potential outcome. A treated unit reveals
$Y_i(1)$; its $Y_i(0)$, what would have happened \textbf{without} treatment, is the
\textbf{missing counterfactual}.
\end{alertblock}

- Individual effects $\tau_i$ are not identified; the targets are **averages over
  groups**.
- Notation: $\E[\,\cdot\mid D_i=1\,]$ is the average **among treated** units,
  $\E[\,\cdot\mid D_i=0\,]$ the average **among untreated** units.

## The target: the average effect on the treated

\begin{block}{Average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)}
$$ \text{ATT}=\E[\,Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid D_i=1\,]. $$
\end{block}

- The effect for the units that **were** treated: did the policy change the outcome of
  its recipients?
- The average effect on the **untreated**, $\E[\,Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid D_i=0\,]$, is a
  different parameter when effects are heterogeneous; DiD does not identify it.
- **DiD targets the ATT.** The missing piece is the treated group's untreated
  counterfactual $\E[\,Y_i(0)\mid D_i=1\,]$, which **parallel trends** will supply.

## The two-by-two: two differences

Two groups, two periods — we now index outcomes by time, $Y_{it}(d)$. DiD builds the
treated group's missing counterfactual by assuming it would have moved **like the
control**:

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth]{fig/did_canonical.png}
\end{center}

$$ \widehat{\text{ATT}}=\underbrace{(\bar y_{T,\text{post}}-\bar y_{T,\text{pre}})}_{\text{treated change}}
   -\underbrace{(\bar y_{C,\text{post}}-\bar y_{C,\text{pre}})}_{\text{control change}} $$

## Parallel trends: the identifying assumption

\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.64\textwidth}
\begin{alertblock}{Parallel trends}
Had the treated group \emph{not} been treated, its outcome would have changed over time by
the \textbf{same amount} as the control group. Writing $\Delta Y_i(0)$ for that change in
the \textbf{untreated} outcome:
$$ \E[\Delta Y_i(0)\mid D_i=1]=\E[\Delta Y_i(0)\mid D_i=0]. $$
\end{alertblock}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Levels} may differ (fixed effects absorb them); only the \textbf{trend}
must match.
\item \textbf{Untestable} (an unobserved counterfactual): defended with pre-period
evidence and economic argument, never proved.
\item \textbf{No anticipation}, the companion assumption: treated units do not respond
before the date, so their pre-period outcome is $Y_i(0)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.34\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig/para.png}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

## The regression form

The $2\times2$ DiD is one OLS regression:
$$ y_{it}=\alpha+\gamma\,D_i+\lambda\,\text{Post}_t+\beta\,(D_i\times\text{Post}_t)+\varepsilon_{it}. $$

- $\gamma$ — the fixed treated-vs-control gap; $\lambda$ — the common time shock.
- **$\beta$ — the DiD coefficient, equal to the ATT** under parallel trends; the
  interaction $D_i\times\text{Post}_t$ equals $d_{it}$.
- Most of the time this standard DiD is estimated with a TWFE:
$$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\beta\,d_{it}+u_{it}. $$

## Example: Card and Krueger (1994)

New Jersey raised its minimum wage (1992); neighbouring Pennsylvania did not. Compare
fast-food employment across the state line.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
FTE employment & Before & After & Change\\
\midrule
New Jersey (treated) & 20.44 & 21.03 & $+0.59$\\
Pennsylvania (control) & 23.33 & 21.17 & $-2.16$\\
\midrule
\textbf{Difference-in-differences} & & & $\mathbf{+2.76}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Employment in New Jersey **rose** relative to Pennsylvania — not just "did not fall" —
  against the textbook competitive prediction.
- The cross-border design makes parallel trends plausible: similar labour markets, same
  macro shocks — the control was chosen for that reason (next section).

# Comparison group

## Designing the comparison

Parallel trends is an assumption on the **shocks**: absent the policy, the treated and the
comparison group would have received the same ones. The choice of the comparison group is
part of the identification strategy and is made on economic grounds before estimation.

1. **Common shocks.** Same industry, markets and geography, so that the time effect
   $f_t$ is common to both groups, with no shock specific to one group during the
   estimation window.
2. **No spillovers (SUTVA).** The policy does not change the outcome of the comparison
   group. Identify the channel of the policy (a price, a quantity, a payment) and verify
   that it did not move for that group.
3. **No anticipation.** The treated group does not respond before the date. Otherwise the
   pre-period already contains part of the effect.
4. **No selection on a temporary shock.** Units may differ from the control group in
   level, but they must not enter treatment because their outcome has just changed
   temporarily. Example: Ashenfelter's dip (Ashenfelter, 1978). Workers enter a training
   programme because their earnings have just fallen, and these earnings would have
   recovered anyway.

# Dynamics

## The event-study specification

Replace the single switch by a full set of **leads and lags** around each unit's treatment
date:
$$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\sum_{k\neq -1}\beta_k\,\mathbf{1}\{t-t^*_i=k\}\,D_i+u_{it}. $$

- $k=t-t^*_i$ is **event time** ($t^*_i$ = the treatment date); $k=-1$ is the **omitted
  baseline**, so each $\beta_k$ is relative to the period just before treatment.
- $\beta_k$ for $k<0$ are **pre-trends**; for $k\ge0$ they are **dynamic treatment
  effects**.
- With one treatment date this is simply one coefficient per **calendar year** on the
  treated dummy.

## Reading the event study

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{fig/event_study.png}
\end{center}

- **Flat, near-zero** coefficients before $0$ are consistent with parallel trends; the
  post coefficients trace the effect's **dynamics**.
- A sloping pre-period ($\beta_k\neq0$ for $k<0$) is a failure of parallel trends before
  treatment: the comparison group has to be revised.

## A caution on pre-trends

\begin{block}{Passing a pre-trend test is reassuring, not decisive}
Tests of $\beta_k=0$ for $k<0$ often have \textbf{low power} — they miss real violations —
and conditioning on "passing" can itself distort the estimate (Roth, 2022).
\end{block}

- Treat them as **evidence**, alongside an economic case for why the trends should align.
- **Plot** the coefficients; never rely on a single $p$-value (on event-study design and
  visualization, see Freyaldenhoven et al. 2021).

# Diagnostics

## Sensitivity analysis: Rambachan and Roth (2023)

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.80\textwidth]{fig/sensitivity.png}
\end{center}

\vspace{-4pt}
\footnotesize
- **(a)** Pre-trend test fails. The largest change from one year to the next is 0.8. If
  the gap kept changing that much after the policy (grey band, $\bar M = 1$), the
  estimated effects would still lie far outside the band.
- **(b)** The bars stay below zero up to $\bar M \approx 8$. Despite the failed pre-trend
  test, the conclusion that the policy lowered the outcome holds, because the violation
  of parallel trends is small compared with the effect. A bar crossing zero already at
  $\bar M < 1$ would mean that changes as large as those observed before the policy could
  explain the whole effect.

## Placebo tests

A design that identifies an effect where there is one should find **nothing** where there
is none:

- **Placebo in time** — apply the design to a date at which nothing happened, inside the
  pre-period.
- **Placebo group** — apply the design to a group that could not have been affected.
- **Placebo outcome** — an outcome the policy cannot reach through the claimed channel.

\vspace{4pt}
A placebo in time is a $2\times2$ on pre-treatment years, a linear combination of the
pre-period coefficients: a rejection is a failure of parallel trends at that date. Placebo
groups and outcomes test the channel: a rejection means some other shock separates the
groups. Both belong in the paper.

## Composition: the balanced-panel check

Units enter and leave panels — and **leaving can be an effect** of the policy (firms close,
farms exit, workers move).

- In the full sample the post-period mean is computed on **survivors**; if the leavers were
  the losers, the effect appears to fade faster than it does for any given unit.
- **Check:** re-estimate on units present in every year of a window around the policy
  (a *balanced* panel).
- Report **both**. They answer different questions: the balanced panel gives the effect
  on the units that stay, the full panel the effect on the observed population,
  composition included. The direction of the gap depends on who leaves.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.30\textwidth]{fig/survivorship_plane.png}
\end{center}

# Inference

## Autocorrelation and standard errors

A DiD panel follows the same units for many years. Within a unit, two variables change
little from one year to the next:

- the outcome $y_{it}$, which is autocorrelated (panel chapter);
- the treatment $d_{it}$, which equals 1 in every year after the policy.

The years of one unit are therefore not independent observations, and standard errors that
treat them as independent are too small.

- **Solution** (Bertrand et al., 2004). Cluster the standard errors at the level at which
  the treatment is assigned. If each firm is treated or not, cluster by firm: all its
  years form one cluster, and the correlation between them is allowed.
- When the policy is assigned to whole groups of units (all the firms of a region),
  cluster by that group, because its units share the treatment and its shocks.
- Report $G$, the number of clusters. The estimator requires a large $G$.

## One treated group

Many DiDs have a single treated group: a sector, a state, a country. Two problems follow
for the standard errors.

- Clustering at the level of treatment assignment gives $G=2$ clusters, the treated group
  and the comparison group. The cluster-robust estimator requires a large $G$ and cannot
  be used.
- Clustering by unit ignores the shock that hits the whole treated group in a given year
  (a price cycle, an embargo). With one treated group this shock does not average out,
  and the standard errors are too small.

1. **Placebo in time.** Estimate the same DiD at dates before the policy, when the true
   effect is zero. The estimates obtained show how large an effect the shocks alone
   produce.
2. **Permutation test.** When several untreated groups are available, assign the
   treatment to each of them in turn and re-estimate. If the true estimate is larger than
   almost all of these placebo estimates, the shocks alone are unlikely to explain it
   (Conley and Taber, 2011; Ferman and Pinto, 2019).

# Conclusion

## Conclusion

1. The objective of a DiD analysis is to estimate the average effect of a policy on the
   treated group (ATT). It is identified under parallel trends and no anticipation.
2. The comparison group is chosen on economic grounds, before estimation: common shocks,
   no spillovers, no anticipation, no Ashenfelter's dip.
3. The $2\times2$ gives one average effect. The event study gives the dynamic effect.
4. The result is then checked with the pre-period coefficients, a sensitivity analysis,
   placebo tests and a balanced panel.

# Applied

## Build the treatment variables

Six lines create the treatment variables, the region $\times$ year cell, the sample and
the clustering.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
df["lait"] = (df["groupe"] == "lait").astype(int)            # 1
df["post"] = (df["annee"] >= 2015).astype(int)               # 2
df["d"]    = df["lait"] * df["post"]                         # 3
df["reg_an"] = df["region"].astype(str) + "_" \
             + df["annee"].astype(str)                       # 4
base = df[df["groupe"].isin(["lait", "caprins"])]            # 5
cl = {"CRV1": "id"}                                          # 6
```

\small

- **1**, **2** — $D_i$, 1 for a dairy farm, and $\text{Post}_t$, 1 from 2015 on;
  `.astype(int)` turns `True`/`False` into 1/0.
- **3** — $d_{it} = D_i \times \text{Post}_t$: the regressor whose coefficient is the ATT.
- **4** — a text label such as `"22_2015"`, one per region and year; its fixed effect
  compares dairy and goat farms of the **same region the same year**.
- **5** — keeps the treated group and its control; `.isin` tests membership in a list.
- **6** — standard errors clustered by farm, passed to every regression as `vcov=cl`.

## The $2\times2$: by hand, then in regression

Five lines reproduce the table of four means and three regression versions, equal only
in a balanced panel.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
w = base[base["annee"].between(2012, 2016)]                   # 1
tab = w.groupby(["groupe","post"])["res_uta"].mean().unstack() # 2
m1 = pf.feols("res_uta ~ lait + post + lait:post", w, vcov=cl) # 3
m2 = pf.feols("res_uta ~ d | id + annee", w, vcov=cl)          # 4
m3 = pf.feols("res_uta ~ d | id + reg_an", w, vcov=cl)         # 5
```

\small

- **1** — three years before, two years after.
- **2** — the mean outcome by group and period, `unstack()` putting the two periods
  side by side: the $2\times2$ table. The DiD is the difference of the two row changes.
- **3** — the same number as a regression: `lait:post` is the interaction, its
  coefficient is $\beta$; `lait` and `post` alone are $\gamma$ and $\lambda$.
- **4** — with farm and year fixed effects: each farm compared to itself.
- **5** — with region $\times$ year effects instead of year effects: neighbours only.

## The event study

Three lines estimate one coefficient per year and read them.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
sc = base[~base["annee"].isin(range(2007, 2012))]             # 1
es = pf.feols("res_uta ~ i(annee, lait, ref=2014) | id + reg_an",
              sc, vcov=cl)                                    # 2
es.coef()                                                     # 3
```

\small

- **1** — drops the years 2007 to 2011, the dairy cycle excluded ex ante; `~` negates
  the condition.
- **2** — `i(annee, lait, ref=2014)` builds one dummy per year, **multiplied by** the
  treated indicator, and leaves 2014 out as the reference. The coefficient of each
  dummy is $\beta_k$: the dairy-minus-goat gap in that year, relative to 2014.
- **3** — the coefficients, named `annee::2015:lait` and so on. The years before 2015
  are the pre-trend check, the years after trace the effect. The four-digit year can be
  read out of each name with a regular expression.

## Pre-trend test, placebo date, balanced panel

Three groups of lines produce the checks of the chapter.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
b = es.coef()[pre]; V = es._vcov[np.ix_(idx, idx)]            # 1
W = b @ np.linalg.solve(V, b)                                 # 2
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(W, len(b))                             # 3
pl = base[base["annee"].between(2000, 2006)].copy()           # 4
pl["d_pl"] = pl["lait"] * (pl["annee"] >= 2004).astype(int)   # 5
bal = base[base["id"].isin(ids_bal)
           & base["annee"].between(2012, 2018)]               # 6
```

\small

- **1** to **3** — the joint test that all pre-2015 coefficients are zero. `pre` lists
  their names, `idx` their positions; `b` is the vector of estimates, `V` their covariance
  block (`np.ix_` selects it); `W = b'V^{-1}b` is the Wald statistic, $\chi^2$ under
  $H_0$ with as many degrees of freedom as coefficients.
- **4**, **5** — the placebo: pre-period only, a fake treatment date in 2004; the
  coefficient of `d_pl` should be near zero.
- **6** — the balanced panel: `ids_bal` lists the farms present every year from 2012 to
  2018; the sample keeps them over those years, so the set of farms observed no longer
  changes.
